name: Achilles Tendon Rupture
summary: Partial or complete rupture of the Achilles tendon, commonly presenting with sudden posterior-ankle pain and loss of plantar-flexion function.

looksLike: Difficulty walking or rising onto toes
redFlags: Suspected rupture requires prompt medical/orthopaedic pathway
firstSteps: Immobilize in plantar flexion/equinus according to local protocol

tests.name: Thompson (Calf-Squeeze) Test
tests.positive: Absent or markedly reduced plantar flexion during calf squeeze.

tests.name: Matles Test
tests.purpose: Assess resting ankle position for tendon discontinuity.
tests.positive: Injured ankle falls toward more dorsiflexion / less resting plantar flexion.

stages.label: Immediate Protection & Referral
stages.goal: Protect tendon length and enter an evidence-based operative or nonoperative pathway.
do: Immobilize in plantar flexion/equinus according to local protocol
Shared decision-making regarding operative vs nonoperative management
dose: Maintain safe hip/knee/toe ROM and general conditioning as allowed by the treating protocol

stages.label: Protected Functional Rehabilitation
stages.goal: Restore safe weight bearing and controlled motion without tendon elongation.
do: Boot/wedges and weight-bearing progression per protocol
dose: Isometric plantar flexion: multiple low-to-moderate effort holds when cleared

stages.label: Calf Strength Restoration
stages.goal: Rebuild plantar-flexor strength and tendon load capacity.
do: Progress seated to standing calf loading
Double- to single-leg heel raise progression
dose: Calf raises: 3–5 x 6–15 with progressive load

stages.label: Energy Storage & Return
stages.goal: Restore hopping, running and sport/work demands.
dose: Running volume and speed progressed gradually

returnCriteria: Repeated single-leg heel raises with good height
Clinician/orthopaedic clearance for high-demand sport when required

investigations: Diagnosis is often clinical when Thompson and examination are clear.
Ultrasound or MRI may help when findings are equivocal, partial tear is suspected or surgical planning requires it.
manual: Do not aggressively mobilize into dorsiflexion early or stretch the healing tendon beyond protocol.
Later joint/soft-tissue techniques may address secondary stiffness once tendon protection allows.
Scar mobilization may be considered after surgical wound healing.
modalities: Modalities are secondary to protection and progressive loading.
Compression may help swelling when medically appropriate.
Monitor for DVT signs during immobilization.
mistakes: Treating rupture like simple Achilles tendinopathy
Progressing running before calf capacity is restored
pearls: Calf squeeze with no plantar flexion = Achilles rupture until proven otherwise.
Operative and nonoperative pathways both require structured rehabilitation.

tests.name: Thompson (Calf-Squeeze) Test
tests.positive: Absent or markedly reduced plantar flexion during calf squeeze.
tests.patientPosition: Prone with feet beyond the edge of the plinth, or kneeling with feet unsupported.
tests.therapistPosition: At the foot of the tested side.
tests.handPlacement: Both hands around the calf muscle belly.
procedure: Observe the foot for plantar flexion.
Compare with the opposite side if uncertain.
tests.clinicalNote: A positive Thompson test can establish strong clinical suspicion; imaging is not automatically required when the examination is clear.

tests.name: Matles Test
tests.purpose: Assess resting ankle position for tendon discontinuity.
tests.positive: Injured ankle falls toward more dorsiflexion / less resting plantar flexion.
tests.patientPosition: Prone with both knees flexed to about 90°.
tests.therapistPosition: At the foot of the table.
tests.handPlacement: No special hand placement; observe ankle resting position.
procedure: Compare resting ankle position side to side.
tests.interpretation: Supports Achilles rupture when combined with other findings.

story.headline: Who kicked my heel? The mystery with nobody behind you
story.scene: A weekend badminton player pushes off to reach a shot. He looks behind him: 'Someone kicked me!' Nobody is there. He struggles to push off and cannot manage a single-leg heel rise.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'Maybe it's a calf cramp?' Therapist: 'A cramp is possible in some stories. This one needs an Achilles check first.'
story.clue: A sudden kick-like sensation, weak plantar flexion and an abnormal calf-squeeze response raise concern for Achilles rupture.
story.twist: Some people with a ruptured Achilles can still point their toes using other muscles. Active plantar flexion alone does not rule out rupture.
story.aha: The tendon can be seriously injured even when the patient can move the foot a little.
story.patientTranslation: The strong tendon behind your ankle may have torn. This needs prompt medical assessment and a protected treatment pathway—not a vigorous massage or stretching session.
story.clinicianReasoning: Assess calf squeeze/Thompson response and resting ankle angle alongside history, tendon palpation and neurovascular status. Urgently direct suspected rupture into an appropriate immobilization and orthopaedic pathway.
story.rehabBridge: First: protect and obtain a specialist plan. Later: staged loading, calf strength and eventually propulsion, within the selected operative or nonoperative protocol.
story.question: A patient felt kicked in the heel, cannot push off and shows no plantar flexion on calf squeeze. Best action?
options: Protect and arrange prompt medical/orthopaedic assessment for suspected rupture
story.explanation: This cluster is concerning for complete Achilles rupture. Prompt assessment and protection are more important than provocative rehabilitation.
